- Patient has verified **identity, site, procedure, and consent** [5][7]
- **Site is marked**, or marking not applicable [5][7]
- **Anaesthesia machine and medication check** complete [5]
- **Pulse oximeter** on the patient and functioning [5][7]
- **Known allergy?** — all team members aware [5][7]
- **Difficult airway / aspiration risk?** — if yes, equipment and assistance available [5][7]

- Confirm **patient's name, procedure, and where the incision will be made** [2][5][7]

  - **Anaesthetist:** any patient-specific concerns [5][7]

## Why normothermia matters

**It is a strong, high-quality recommendation.** The CDC recommends maintaining perioperative normothermia as a **Category IA (strong recommendation, high-to-moderate quality evidence)** [1], and ERAS gynecologic oncology guidelines rate it **evidence level high, recommendation grade strong**, stating maintenance of normothermia should be incorporated into all ERAS programs [3].

**Why patients are at risk:** during anesthesia and major surgery there is a high risk of hypothermia because of exposure plus impairment of the normal thermoregulatory response, which accelerates heat loss [2].

**Harms of hypothermia:**
- **Surgical site infection (SSI)** — hypothermia is linked to increased SSI risk [3][8]; one prospective randomized colorectal study found intra-operative hypothermia **tripled** wound infection (p=0.009) [4]. Active warming vs conventional methods gives an **absolute risk reduction of 13%** for wound infection [2]. A trial extending warming to **2 hours before and after surgery** in major abdominal surgery reduced SSI from **27% to 13% (p=0.027)** — roughly halved [6][3][8]. A systematic review found forced air warming benefited SSI/complication rates in abdominal surgery (**RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.20–0.66**) [7].
- **Cardiac events** — hypothermia increases cardiac morbidity [2]; maintaining normothermia reduces perioperative morbid cardiac events in major operations [5][3].
- **Coagulation and bleeding** — hypothermia adversely affects coagulation and increases bleeding [2].
- **Drug metabolism** — impaired by hypothermia [2].
- **Postoperative shivering** — increases oxygen consumption at a critical time and can worsen pain [2].

**Practical points from the evidence (to support, not replace, your judgement):**
- Warm **actively throughout the perioperative period, including prewarming**, to avoid the initial temperature drop [2]; prewarming with forced air for a **minimum of 45 min** in the holding area yielded higher post-op temperatures than cotton blankets alone [7][6].
- Forced-air blankets are effective and widely used; **underbody warming mattresses** are also effective and avoid a blanket interfering with surgical access — relevant in robotic cases [2].
- **Warm IV fluids** with a suitable device to avoid lowering body temperature [2]; warmed fluids reduce hypothermia alone or combined with forced air warming [7].
- Monitoring: use a device accurate for **core temperature, reliable to ±0.1 °C**, and document temperature continually as part of vital signs; recommended ambient OR temperature **20–25 °C (68–77 °F)** [4] — note this passage is tier 4, not tier 1.

**A gap to be aware of:** the CDC search found **no RCTs** defining the strategies to achieve normothermia, the **lower limit** of normothermia, or the **optimal timing/duration** — these remain unresolved [1]. q: What is the purpose of a postoperative voiding trial?

## Purpose of a Postoperative Voiding Trial

**Core purpose: to confirm the bladder empties adequately after catheter removal, so that postoperative urinary retention is detected before the patient is discharged.**

**Why it matters in gynecologic/urogynecologic patients**
- Women undergoing FPMRS (pelvic reconstructive/incontinence) procedures are **at risk of transient postoperative voiding difficulty** — after midurethral sling surgery only **61% passed the immediate postoperative voiding trial** [1]. The voiding trial identifies that sizeable minority who cannot yet void.
- Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is defined subjectively as inability to void, or objectively as an excessive post-void residual [7]. Undetected retention can cause **bladder overdistention injury, detrusor hypertrophy and overactive voiding symptoms**, which are distressing to patients [7]. Reported POUR incidence across surgical procedures ranges **3–70%** [7]; adult bladder capacity is **400–600 mL** [7].
- It supports **early catheter removal** (preferably within **3–8 h**), which shortens length of stay and lowers infection risk but modestly increases recatheterization risk — so if an early trial without catheter is done, **post-void residuals should be monitored prior to discharge** [1].

**How a pass/fail is operationalised (one published protocol)**
- In a laparoscopic gynecologic surgery RCT, a **successful void = any voided volume >100 mL**, or a void <100 mL with a **bladder-scan residual <100 mL**; a **failed trial = voided <100 mL with >100 mL residual** [2]. Your unit's own algorithm and thresholds take precedence.

**Related practical points from the evidence**
- **Patient-reported force of urinary stream** correlates well with measured voided volume and may be an alternative to PVR checks [1]. Patient-driven self-discontinuation of a transurethral catheter is another alternative to inpatient/office trial without catheter [1].
- **Retrograde bladder filling (backfilling)** shortens time to first void and PACU/discharge times, and in pelvic reconstructive/incontinence surgery it improved trial-of-void success rates and more accurately predicted voiding dysfunction than spontaneous voiding, with similar patient satisfaction [3].
- **Which patients actually need a voiding trial is not settled** and is often left to surgeon judgement; one retrospective cohort of ~5000 same-day gynecologic surgery patients found no difference in readmission or retention with vs. without a void-before-discharge order, but did not account for procedure type [4].
- Prolonged catheterization should only be used where there are **specific indications** [1].

## Why early mobilisation matters after gynaecological surgery

**It is a core element of enhanced recovery (ER), not an optional extra**

- Early mobilisation is described as "key" to enhanced recovery in gynaecology, and is achievable **regardless of age** provided the woman gets appropriate education and support [1].
- It sits alongside the other ER elements: early feeding, reduced routine IV fluid volumes, pain optimisation, anti-emetics and laxatives, and early discharge planning [1][2].

2. **Reduces thromboembolism risk** — early mobilisation reduces the risk of VTE [1]. NICE NG89 makes this a nursing care point: encourage people to mobilise as soon as possible, and do not allow people to become dehydrated unless clinically indicated [6].
3. **Contributes to shorter length of stay and higher patient satisfaction** — as part of the wider ER pathway, which reduces the physiological stress response and organ dysfunction caused by surgery, giving more rapid recovery and quicker return to normal activity [1][8].

**Why this matters especially in gynae-oncology**

- VTE risk is high after gynaecological cancer surgery: 6–7% of patients despite LMWH prophylaxis, and a malignancy increases post-operative VTE fourfold versus benign disease [5]. In ovarian cancer debulking, 1 in 7 women developed post-operative VTE [7].
- Risk persists after discharge — most post-operative VTE occurs after the first post-operative week, and 40% of gynae-cancer patients who develop VTE do so more than 21 days after surgery [3], which is why guidelines recommend **extended prophylaxis (28 days) with LMWH** after pelvic/abdominal cancer surgery [5]. - Enhanced recovery programmes and improved surgical technique may themselves modify VTE risk [4]; in one ovarian cancer study, fast-track patients (epidural analgesia, early oral feeding, early mobilisation) were discharged earlier, which may reduce VTE risk — though VTE rates were not directly measured [2]. Note the evidence base has a shortage of randomised controlled trials [2].

## Practical enablers on the ward

- **Effective analgesia within a protocol using reduced systemic opiates** is what makes early mobilisation possible — pain control is the lever [1].
- **Remove catheters, drains, vaginal packs and IV drips as soon as possible**, both to enable mobilisation and to prevent associated secondary infections [1].
- **After catheter removal, monitor voiding with post-void residual checks** — women are at risk of short-term voiding problems after pelvic surgery. If needed, it is safe to discharge with an indwelling catheter and arrange an outpatient trial without catheter [1].
- **Maintain hydration** unless clinically contraindicated [6].

## Limits of this evidence

**Definition**

ERAS pathways are specially designed **multimodal perioperative care pathways** intended to achieve rapid recovery after major surgery by supporting preoperative organ function and attenuating the stress response caused by surgical trauma, so patients return to normal activities as soon as possible [3][4]. - Preoperative components [3][4]
- Perioperative/intraoperative components [3][4]
- Postoperative components [3][4]

- NICE NG180: **offer an enhanced recovery programme to people having elective major or complex surgery** [6].

**2. Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene**

- If hands are washed with a **non-antimicrobial soap**, skin bacteria proliferate **rapidly** under surgical gloves; this process is **slowed** after preoperative washing with a medicated soap [1].
- Hand hygiene is **required regardless of whether gloves are used or changed** [7]. Failure to remove gloves after patient contact, or between "dirty" and "clean" body-site care on the same patient, counts as **non-adherence** to hand-hygiene recommendations [7].

**3. Who must scrub, and when**

Surgical team members who have **direct contact with the sterile operating field or with sterile instruments/supplies used in the field** wash hands and forearms (the surgical scrub) **immediately before donning sterile gowns and gloves** [3].

**4. What agent characteristics matter**

The optimal scrub antiseptic should have a **broad spectrum of activity, be fast-acting, and have a persistent effect** [3]. Agents available for this purpose contain alcohol, chlorhexidine, iodine/iodophors, para-chloro-meta-xylenol, or triclosan; alcohol is regarded as the gold standard for surgical hand preparation in several European countries, while **povidone-iodine and chlorhexidine gluconate** are the agents of choice for most US surgical team members [3]. ## Risk Factors for Surgical Site Infection (SSI)

The evidence groups these into **patient factors** and **operation/procedure factors**.

### Patient-related factors
- **Coincident remote-site infection** — an infection elsewhere in the body at the time of surgery [1]. Knowing this preoperatively may allow the surgical team to reduce risk by rescheduling the operation [4].
- **Colonization**, particularly nasal (nares) colonization with *S. aureus* [1]
- **Diabetes mellitus** — SSI rates are reported as **two to three times higher** than in patients without diabetes [2]; diabetes is also associated with increased SSI risk in meta-analysis of prospective cohorts [3]
- **Cigarette smoking / tobacco use** [1][7]
- **Systemic steroid use** [1]
- **Obesity — BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²** [1]
- **Extremes of age** [1][7]
- **Poor nutritional status / malnutrition** [1][7]
- **Perioperative blood transfusion** [1]
- **Prolonged preoperative hospital stay** [1]; prolonged *postoperative* stay is also associated with SSI, though this is probably a surrogate marker for severity of illness and comorbidity rather than a cause [1]
- Impaired host resistance generally — SSI risk is conceptualised as bacterial dose × virulence ÷ host resistance, with acute and chronic host liabilities reducing defences [5]

### Operation-related factors
- **Degree of bacterial contamination of the wound** at the time of procedure [7]; probability of infection rises proportionally with the number and virulence of organisms [5]
- **Emergency surgery** [7]
- **Local wound characteristics** — residual dead tissue, dead space, sutures or other foreign material [5][2]
- **Intraoperative technique factors**: inadequate haemostasis or blood supply, hypothermia, rough tissue handling, inadvertent entry into a hollow viscus, retained devitalized tissue, and inappropriate use of drains/suture material [2]
- **Preoperative preparation shortfalls** — absence of antiseptic showering, hair removal by **shaving rather than clipping**, and inadequate skin prep or hand/forearm scrub antisepsis [1]
- **Surgical/provider volume** has also been studied as a risk determinant [3]

### Practical notes for your shift
- Many of these factors are **not modifiable**, but the majority of SSIs are still considered **preventable** [7].
- SSIs occur in **2%–4%** of inpatient surgical patients and are defined by CDC/NHSN as infection at or near the incision within **30 to 90 days**, depending on procedure type — relevant when counselling patients on what to watch for after discharge [8].
- **Maintaining normothermia** during major operations also reduces perioperative cardiac events [6]; the benefit of high (80% vs 30–35%) inspired oxygen is **unresolved** — trials conflict and no conclusion can be drawn, though it is "almost certainly not harmful" [6].

q: What is the role of intermittent pneumatic compression?
answer:
## Role of intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC)

**What it is / how it works**
IPC is a mechanical method of VTE prophylaxis using an air pump plus inflatable garments to improve venous circulation in the lower limbs of people at risk of DVT or PE [1]. The inflation–deflation cycle mimics the normal ambulatory pump action of the thigh, calf and foot, increasing both the volume and rate of blood flow, eliminating venous stasis and replicating the natural muscle pump [1]. Garments may be thigh- or knee-length sleeves wrapped around the leg, or a foot garment designed to mimic walking [1].

**Main advantage and drawbacks**
The key advantage is the absence of an associated bleeding risk, which makes it useful when anticoagulation is contraindicated [6]. Drawbacks are potential interference with ambulation and the need to keep the devices in place nearly continuously [6]. Graduated compression stockings can be used in conjunction with an IPC device [6].

**Where it is indicated in the evidence provided**
- **Alternative to anti-embolism stockings:** if stockings must be stopped because of skin marking, blistering, discolouration (particularly over heels and bony prominences), or pain/discomfort, offer IPC as an alternative if suitable [3].
- **Major/serious trauma:** offer mechanical prophylaxis with IPC on admission, continuing until the person no longer has significantly reduced mobility relative to their normal or anticipated mobility [4]. Reassess VTE and bleeding risk whenever the clinical condition changes and at least daily [4]. Trauma guidance elsewhere recommends early IPC while the patient is immobile and has a bleeding risk (Grade 1C), then combined pharmacological + IPC prophylaxis within 24 h after bleeding is controlled and until mobile (Grade 1B) [8].
- **Open vascular surgery / major endovascular procedures (incl. EVAR):** consider mechanical prophylaxis on admission if pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated — either anti-embolism stockings or IPC — continued until mobility is no longer significantly reduced [5].
- **Acute stroke:** stockings are *not* offered [2]; consider IPC for people who are immobile, started **within 3 days** of the acute stroke, and provided for **30 days or until the person is mobile or discharged, whichever is sooner** [2]. Counselling should explain it reduces DVT risk and may increase survival chances, but will not aid stroke recovery and there may be an associated increased risk of surviving with severe disability [2].

**Practical/safety points for your shift**
- Do **not** offer IPC to anyone with a known allergy to the material of manufacture [3].
- Advise the person to wear the device for as much time as possible [3].
- If stockings are in use alongside, remove them daily for hygiene and skin inspection; inspect 2–3 times a day (especially heels and bony prominences) where there is significantly reduced mobility, poor skin integrity or sensory loss [3].

**Gap for your gynaecology setting:** the passages given do not state a specific IPC recommendation for gynaecologic or urogynecologic surgery. The urogynaecology consensus notes VTE is potentially preventable, that 10–40% of gynaecological procedures are complicated by VTE without thromboprophylaxis, that urogynaecological surgery is low-to-moderate risk (incidence 0.1–0.3%), and that individual risk should be assessed preoperatively (e.g. Caprini score), with risk factors including immobility, older age, obesity and smoking — but it does not specify the IPC regimen in the text provided [7]. Please use local protocol and your own assessment for the specific patient.
